sections.heading: User Input
sections.body: You have already learned that printf() is used to output values in C. To get user input, you can use the scanf() function:

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: Output a number entered by the user: The scanf() function takes two arguments: the format specifier of the variable (%d in the example above) and the reference operator (&myNum), which stores the memory address of the variable. Tip: You will learn more about memory addresses and functions in the next chapter.

Take String Input
sections.body: You can also get a string entered by the user:

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: Output the name of a user: Note: When working with strings in scanf(), you must specify the size of the string/array (we used a very high number, 30 in our example, but at least then we are certain it will store enough characters for the first name), and you don't have to use the reference operator (&). However, the scanf() function has some limitations: it considers space (whitespace, tabs, etc) as a terminating character, which means that it can only display a single word (even if you type many words). For example:

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: From the example above, you would expect the program to print "John Doe", but it only prints "John". That's why, when working with strings, we often use the fgets() function to read a line of text. Note that you must include the following arguments: the name of the string variable, sizeof(string_name), and stdin:

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: Use the scanf() function to get a single word as input, and use fgets() for multiple words.
